## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

{{< include ../learning_objectives/0680-containers-platforms.qmd >}}

## One image, one kind of processor

An image holds programs compiled for one kind of processor.
Macs with Apple silicon, and some Windows laptops, have ARM processors (`arm64`).
Most other laptops, and GitHub's usual Linux computers, have Intel or AMD processors (`amd64`).
`docker build` builds for the computer it runs on,
so the `hello-cowsay` image from [Building images](0630-containers-building.qmd),
built on a Mac with Apple silicon, is for `arm64` only:

```bash
docker image inspect hello-cowsay --format '{{.Os}}/{{.Architecture}}'
```

```out
linux/arm64
```

A classmate with an Intel laptop could not use it as it is,
just as an ARM computer cannot pull the older `rocker/tidyverse` images
(see the warning in [Building images](0630-containers-building.qmd)).

## Build for both kinds on your computer

`--platform` builds the image for each platform you list.
Here are the steps of building `hello-cowsay` for both:

```bash
docker build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --tag hello-cowsay .
```

```out
[+] Building 65.7s (9/9) FINISHED                                              docker:desktop-linux
 => [linux/arm64 internal] load metadata for docker.io/rocker/r-ver:4.6.2                      0.1s
 => [linux/amd64 internal] load metadata for docker.io/rocker/r-ver:4.6.2                      1.4s
 => [linux/amd64 1/2] FROM docker.io/rocker/r-ver:4.6.2@sha256:8739c76d2d9316698a7145b032601  51.0s
 => [linux/arm64 1/2] FROM docker.io/rocker/r-ver:4.6.2@sha256:8739c76d2d9316698a7145b032601f  0.0s
 => CACHED [linux/arm64 2/2] RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"                       0.0s
 => [linux/amd64 2/2] RUN Rscript -e "install.packages('cowsay')"                             12.7s
```

The `arm64` steps were already cached.
For `amd64`, Docker downloaded the `amd64` version of `rocker/r-ver:4.6.2`,
and ran the `RUN` step by emulating an Intel processor,
which is slower than running it on one.
`docker image ls --tree` shows that the one tag now has both:

```bash
docker image ls --tree hello-cowsay
```

```out
IMAGE                 ID             DISK USAGE   CONTENT SIZE   EXTRA
hello-cowsay:latest   fcb420e64e33       1.86GB          800MB        
├─ linux/amd64        7f260b562e1c        410MB          410MB        
└─ linux/arm64        f2d1c5ab15c8       1.45GB          390MB        
```

`--platform` on `docker run` picks which one to run,
and `uname -m` prints the processor the container sees:

```bash
docker run --rm --platform linux/amd64 hello-cowsay uname -m
docker run --rm --platform linux/arm64 hello-cowsay uname -m
```

```out
x86_64
aarch64
```

Docker's guide to [multi-platform builds](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/)
has the details, including what your Docker needs to build them.

## Push both to Docker Hub

To share the image, push it to a container registry such as [Docker Hub](https://hub.docker.com/),
where you need a free account.
The image's name must start with your Docker Hub username,
so replace `USERNAME` below with yours:

<!-- TODO: dan: run with your Docker Hub account and add the output; Claude checked the same commands against a registry on localhost (both platforms were pushed under one tag) -->

```bash
docker login
docker tag hello-cowsay USERNAME/hello-cowsay:0.1
docker push USERNAME/hello-cowsay:0.1
```

- `docker login` signs you in to Docker Hub.
- `docker tag` gives the image a second name, with your username and a version, `0.1`.
- `docker push` uploads it.
  Because the image has both platforms, it uploads both, under the one tag.

::: {.callout-note title="Signing in with `docker login`"}
`docker login` signs you in through your web browser.
It prints a one-time code and opens Docker's sign-in page,
where you confirm the code and sign in,
so you never type your password in the terminal.

`docker login -u USERNAME` asks for a password in the terminal instead.
Your Docker Hub password works there,
unless you have turned on two-factor authentication.
Then Docker Hub refuses your password,
and you paste a personal access token at the prompt instead.
[GitHub Actions](1320-github-actions.qmd#github-secrets) shows how to make one.
:::

Anyone can then run `docker pull USERNAME/hello-cowsay:0.1`,
and Docker downloads the version for their computer.
To list the platforms an image in a registry has:

```bash
docker buildx imagetools inspect USERNAME/hello-cowsay:0.1
```

## On GitHub Actions

A project can also build its image on GitHub's computers, every time you push.
[docker-uv-renv](https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv) does this
with [`build-and-render.yml`](https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv/blob/main/.github/workflows/build-and-render.yml):

```{.yaml}
name: Build image and render reports

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:
  build-and-render:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Build the image
        run: docker build --tag docker-uv-renv .

      ## not `make render`: CI has no ssh key to mount
      - name: Render the reports
        run: docker run --rm --volume "$PWD:/workspace" docker-uv-renv uv run quarto render

      ## download them from the run's Summary page
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v7
        with:
          name: reports
          path: |
            reports/*.html
            reports/*.pdf
```

On every push to `main` and every pull request,
a fresh Linux computer (`ubuntu-latest`, an `amd64` computer)
builds the image from the `Dockerfile` in the repository,
renders the reports in a container,
and keeps them for you to download from the run's page,
as in [this run](https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv/actions/runs/43520328267).
Because the build starts from nothing,
it shows that the `Dockerfile` and lockfiles work on a computer other than yours.
GitHub also has ARM computers (`ubuntu-24.04-arm`),
and the project's [`check-platforms.yml`](https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv/blob/main/.github/workflows/check-platforms.yml)
builds the image on both.
Its [`publish-dockerhub.yml`](https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv/blob/main/.github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml)
goes one step further.
It builds the image on both kinds of computer,
publishes it on Docker Hub under one tag, as `docker push` did above,
and writes the new tag into `docker-compose.yml`
(see [Publish the image](https://github.com/chendaniely/docker-uv-renv#publish-the-image) in the project's README).
To sign in to Docker Hub, it needs a Docker Hub access token stored in the repository,
as in [signing in to Docker Hub](1320-github-actions.qmd#github-secrets).
[GitHub Actions](1320-github-actions.qmd) explains how workflow files work.
